questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Membrane Structure Decides Transport
questions.learningObjective: Explain how bilayer structure determines which solutes cross freely
questions.stem: Fabricating a synthetic cell, Priya's brief asks why small polar molecules cross her lipid bilayer far more slowly than small non-polar ones. Which structural feature explains this?

options.text: The polar head groups face inward, so a polar solute has to cross a dry, non-polar fatty acid core.
options.misconception: believes the head groups sit in the bilayer interior

options.text: The non-polar hydrocarbon tails form a water-excluding core that polar solutes cannot easily penetrate.
The phosphate heads are negatively charged and repel the partial positive charge carried by water.
options.misconception: thinks electrostatic repulsion is the main barrier

options.text: The bilayer is only about four nanometres thick, so thickness alone sets the crossing rate.
options.misconception: treats membrane thickness as the sole determinant

questions.explanation: The bilayer interior is non-polar fatty acid tails, so polar molecules cannot shed their water shell there. Non-polar solutes dissolve in the core and pass readily, so the difference follows structure.
questions.hint: Think about what the middle of the bilayer is made of.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Surface Area to Volume Limits a Cell
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how cell division changes total surface area
questions.stem: Sizing a cell capsule, Ravi notes that a spherical cell of radius 4 micrometres has a surface area of about 201 square micrometres. When it divides into two spherical daughter cells of radius 2 micrometres, what is their combined surface area in square micrometres to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: Each daughter cell of radius 2 micrometres has surface area 4 times pi times 4, about 50.27 square micrometres, so together they show 100.53. The increase comes from the smaller radius raising area per unit volume.
questions.hint: Use 4 times pi times r squared for each daughter.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret fluidity data to infer cholesterol behaviour
questions.stem: Testing membrane fluidity in a brief, Nadia measures lateral lipid movement in three bilayers: plain lipid at 20 degrees gives 0.2 units, the same lipid with 12 percent cholesterol gives 0.9, and with 30 percent cholesterol gives 1.4. Which conclusion does this support?

options.text: Cholesterol raises fluidity at this temperature by stopping the fatty acid tails from packing tightly.
options.misconception: treats cholesterol as always stiffening the membrane

options.text: The three membranes are identical apart from the label, so the change must be measurement noise.
options.misconception: dismisses a consistent trend as random error

options.text: Cholesterol buffers the membrane, keeping tails from packing rigidly while also preventing loose packing.
options.misconception: believes cholesterol only ever stiffens membranes

options.text: At 20 degrees the added cholesterol is holding the fatty acid tails apart, so the bilayer moves more freely.

questions.explanation: Permeability and movement both climb as cholesterol is added at 20 degrees, which is below the temperature of tight packing. Cholesterol therefore prevents the tails from rigidifying, though the opposite effect appears above the transition temperature.
questions.hint: Compare the direction of change with what tight packing does.

questions.topic: Cumulative: Four Subunits and Cooperative Binding
questions.learningObjective: Read a cooperative binding diagram and state what it shows
questions.stem: A labelled diagram in the design brief shows a tetrameric enzyme whose four active sites sit at the corners of a square, with the first substrate drawn pushing its neighbouring subunits outward so the other three sites open.

options.text: The first binding event makes the remaining active sites more receptive, so later substrates bind more easily.
The outward shift proves each subunit carries an independent site that is unaffected by its neighbours.
options.misconception: ignores the shape change shown between subunits

options.text: The diagram shows the enzyme reaches maximum activity the moment any one substrate touches a single site.
options.misconception: reads one binding event as full saturation

options.text: The outward shift indicates the subunits are separating to form four separate smaller enzymes.
options.misconception: interprets a conformational shift as subunit dissociation

questions.explanation: The outward push drawn after the first substrate binds is a shape change that improves the fit of the other three sites. That is what cooperative binding means: early events make later ones easier, not independent and not full activity at once.
questions.hint: Look at what happens to the neighbouring sites after binding.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Reading a Diagram of Induced Fit
questions.learningObjective: Correct a claim that an active site is a rigid pre-formed lock
questions.stem: A trainee writes in the design brief that an enzyme's active site is rigid and shaped exactly like its substrate before any binding occurs. Which correction does induced fit require?

options.text: The active site is rigid and reshapes only after the reaction is complete and products have left.
options.misconception: puts the shape change after catalysis

options.text: The enzyme is rigid but the substrate changes shape to slot into a pre-formed site.
options.misconception: moves all flexibility onto the substrate

options.text: The active site is flexible and reshapes as the substrate binds, so the fit is made during binding.
Neither molecule changes shape, and the bond forms wherever the two surfaces happen to touch.
options.misconception: denies conformational change in both partners

questions.explanation: Induced fit means the site is flexible: contact with the substrate triggers a change in shape that tightens the complex and lines up catalytic groups. A pre-shaped rigid site would not explain why small changes in substrate shape can block binding.
questions.hint: Which molecule is described as changing conformation?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: One Amino Acid, One Sticky Surface
questions.learningObjective: Explain how one residue change can abolish binding
questions.stem: The brief notes that a single altered residue in a protein can change its behaviour completely. Explain how one amino acid substitution could destroy the protein's ability to bind its target.

answer.exemplar: The substituted residue may sit in the binding interface and change its charge, size or shape, so the target no longer makes the contacts that anchored it. If the residue lies in the protein's core instead, the substitution can destabilise folding, so the protein loses both structure and function.

questions.explanation: Function rests on shape, and one residue can change charge, polarity or volume. A residue in a binding site loses key contacts, while one in the core destabilises the fold. Either route ends in lost binding.
questions.hint: Consider both the surface and the folded core.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Translating Only Part of a Message
questions.learningObjective: Propose a test that separates a truncated protein from a full-length one
questions.stem: The brief asks how the team could show that only part of a messenger RNA is turned into protein. Propose an experiment that distinguishes a truncated product from a full-length one.

answer.exemplar: Sequence the protein made by the engineered cells and look for an early stop codon, then compare protein size on a gel against a full-length control. Pulse labelling with a marked amino acid followed by immunoprecipitation can confirm which ribosomes finish the transcript. A truncated band smaller than the expected full length supports partial translation.

questions.explanation: A shorter product of the expected kind of sequence points to translation stopping early. Comparing size with a full-length control and checking where the sequence ends are the two observations that separate the two cases.
questions.hint: Compare the product's size and its sequence endpoint.

questions.stem: Mara's brief covers a walled plant cell placed in a strong salt solution whose water potential is more negative than that of the cell sap. Which change in the cell is expected?

options.text: Water leaves by osmosis, the vacuole shrinks and the cell becomes flaccid and soft.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of osmosis

options.text: Solute is pumped out by active transport, so turgor pressure stays constant.
options.misconception: assumes turgor is held steady by pumping

options.text: The wall blocks all water movement, so cell volume and turgor both stay fixed.
options.misconception: treats the cell wall as a waterproof barrier

options.text: Water enters by osmosis, the vacuole swells and turgor pressure rises against the wall.

questions.explanation: A more negative external water potential draws water into the vacuole by osmosis, so the protoplast swells and presses harder on the wall. The wall resists bursting rather than stopping osmosis, and the pressure it resists is turgor.
questions.hint: Compare the water potentials on the two sides.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate flux from permeability and concentration difference
questions.stem: The brief for a lipid-bilayer test cell states a permeability constant of 2.0 times ten to the minus six metres per second for the drug candidate, with a concentration difference of 1.5 moles per cubic metre held across it. What is the net flux in micromoles per square metre per second?
questions.explanation: Flux equals permeability times the concentration difference: 2.0 times ten to the minus six metres per second times 1.5 moles per cubic metre gives 3.0 times ten to the minus six moles per square metre per second, which is 3.0 micromoles.
questions.hint: Use flux equals permeability times concentration difference.

options.text: The rod, whose ratio of about 2.1 per micrometre exceeds the cube's 2.0 and the sphere's 1.87.
The sphere, because a curved surface always exposes more area per unit volume than a flat one.
options.misconception: assumes curvature always raises the ratio

options.text: The cube, because a solid shape keeps its faces flat and its edges sharp.
options.misconception: believes flat faces maximise area per volume

options.text: All three are equal, because the brief states the three cells have identical volumes.
options.misconception: treats equal volume as equal ratio

questions.explanation: Equal volume does not mean equal surface area. The rod reaches about 2.1 per micrometre, the cube 2.0 and the sphere about 1.87, so flattening into a rod raises the ratio and speeds exchange.
questions.hint: Work out the surface area and volume of each shape.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the observation that contradicts independent subunits
questions.stem: In the brief a reviewer states that the four subunits of a tetrameric enzyme each work independently, so binding one substrate cannot affect the others. Which observation contradicts that claim?

options.misconception: repeats the claim as if it were evidence

options.text: Binding the first substrate makes the remaining sites bind faster than they did before it arrived.
The four subunits are chemically identical and assemble into one functional unit.
options.misconception: reads identical subunits as independent behaviour

options.text: The enzyme reaches the same total turnover whether one or four substrates are bound.
options.misconception: confuses identical subunits with equal activity

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Reading a Diagram of Induced Fit
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a flexible site accepts unfamiliar substrates
questions.stem: The brief asks the team to explain, in writing, how an enzyme's active site can fit a substrate that the enzyme has never encountered before.

answer.exemplar: Induced fit means the site is not a rigid lock cut for one key. The flexible loops and side chains around the site test the substrate's shape and then close around it, so contacts never specified in advance are made during binding, and one site can accept a range of related molecules.

questions.explanation: A rigid template would accept only the substrate it was built for. Induced fit explains flexibility: the site reshapes on contact, so one enzyme can accept several related substrates.
questions.hint: Think about a site that is not cut to a single key.

questions.topic: Cumulative: One Amino Acid, One Sticky Surface
questions.learningObjective: Design a test isolating a single residue as the cause of lost binding
questions.stem: Propose an experiment that would show a single amino acid change is responsible for a protein losing its sticky surface, and state the result that would support the claim.

answer.exemplar: Change only the suspected residue back to the original amino acid in the defective protein and restore the sticky surface, then change only that residue in the working protein and destroy it. Measuring binding to the sticky partner before and after each single change isolates that residue, and any change in other properties would show the result is not clean.

questions.explanation: A two-way swap that restores and destroys binding in turn shows the residue is responsible rather than merely correlated. Keeping every other part of the protein and the conditions unchanged removes the alternative explanations.
questions.hint: Change that one residue in both directions.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how one gene can specify more than one protein
questions.stem: In the brief, a lead notes that a single messenger RNA can specify more than one protein. Which mechanism best explains that outcome?

options.text: The message can be spliced in alternative ways, so different sets of exons are kept in the mature RNA.
The message is translated twice, once from the start and once from an internal initiation site.
options.misconception: confuses re-initiation with splicing

options.misconception: treats translation termination as random

options.misconception: invents a second message instead of one

questions.explanation: Alternative splicing keeps different exon combinations in one pre-messenger RNA, so one gene yields several related proteins. Re-initiation changes how much is made, not which parts of the message are used.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Four Subunits and Cooperative Binding
questions.learningObjective: Explain why binding one ligand speeds up later binding
questions.stem: Explain, as the brief requires, why binding of the first ligand to a four-subunit protein makes later bindings faster.

answer.exemplar: Binding in one subunit shifts the shape of the whole tetramer so that neighbouring sites become a closer match for the ligand, lowering the barrier to each later binding event. Because each binding event makes the next one easier, occupancy rises steeply rather than in equal steps, and the sites finally saturate together.

questions.explanation: Cooperativity works through a shared shape change: the first ligand makes the other sites better fits, so each subsequent event faces a lower barrier. That is why the response steepens in the middle of the concentration range.
questions.hint: The subunits influence each other through shape.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Reading a Diagram of Induced Fit
questions.learningObjective: Design a test distinguishing induced fit from a rigid pocket
questions.stem: Propose an experiment that would show an enzyme remodels its active site on substrate binding rather than binding a pre-shaped rigid pocket.

answer.exemplar: Measure the shape of the free enzyme and again with substrate present, for example by crystallography or by following a reporter that reads out the distance between two labelled residues. If that distance changes on substrate addition, the site is flexible and induced fit is real, whereas an unchanged distance would support a rigid pre-formed pocket.

questions.explanation: The two states of the same enzyme give a direct comparison, so any change in shape tied to substrate presence supports induced fit. A rigid pocket would report the same geometry whether or not substrate was bound.
questions.hint: Compare the enzyme shape with and without substrate.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a mostly non-polar steroid sits in a membrane
questions.stem: Explain in writing, as the brief requests, why a steroid such as cholesterol can sit inside a membrane and still alter how the membrane behaves.

answer.exemplar: Cholesterol is built from four fused non-polar carbon rings with only one small polar hydroxyl group, so it can tuck its rings among the fatty acid tails while the hydroxyl stays near the watery surface. Because the rings are bulky and rigid, they occupy space between the tails and change how tightly those tails pack, which is how the membrane's fluidity is buffered.

questions.explanation: A mostly non-polar molecule with one polar end can partition into the bilayer, its rigid rings sitting among the tails and altering how they pack. That is how cholesterol buffers fluidity rather than acting as a channel.

answer.exemplar: Record the amount of ligand bound across a range of ligand concentrations and plot a binding curve. questions.learningObjective: Explain why a transition-state analogue binds tightly
questions.stem: A brief states that an inhibitor resembling the substrate's transition state binds more tightly than the substrate itself. What does this indicate about the enzyme's active site?

questions.explanation: Surface area is 2 times the sum of the three different face areas, so 2 times 56 equals 112 square micrometres, and volume is 8 times 4 times 2, which is 64 cubic micrometres. The ratio is 112 divided by 64, which is 1.75 per micrometre.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: What a Steroid Ring Does in a Membrane
questions.learningObjective: Interpret fluidity data at two temperatures for a buffered membrane
questions.stem: A brief records bilayer fluidity at 10 and 40 degrees Celsius: the cholesterol-free membrane measures 2 and 40 units, while the membrane with 20 percent cholesterol measures 12 and 25 units. Which reading fits both numbers?

options.text: Cholesterol raises fluidity at both temperatures, since the enriched membrane is always faster.
options.misconception: ignores the drop at 40 degrees

options.text: Cholesterol lowers fluidity at both temperatures, since the enriched membrane is always slower.
options.misconception: ignores the rise at 10 degrees

options.text: Cholesterol has no effect on fluidity and the differences come from the phospholipid batch.
options.misconception: dismisses both measured changes as batch effects

options.text: Cholesterol raises fluidity when the membrane is cold and lowers it when the membrane is warm.

questions.explanation: At 10 degrees the enriched membrane is faster and at 40 it is slower, which is a fluidity buffer. Cholesterol hinders tight packing when cold and hinders tail sliding when warm, so it acts both ways.
questions.hint: Compare the enriched membrane with the control at each temperature.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Four Subunits and Cooperative Binding
questions.learningObjective: Read a staged diagram of sequential cooperative binding
questions.stem: Four stages of the same protein are drawn in the brief, with each new ligand shown making the next subunit's site slightly wider. What does the sequence of drawings illustrate?

options.text: Each ligand that binds makes the next site more open, so later ligands bind more readily.
Each ligand takes up fixed space, so later ligands have less room and bind less readily.
options.misconception: describes simple competition rather than cooperation

options.text: All four sites fill at the same moment, so the order shown in the drawing is arbitrary.
options.misconception: ignores the sequential change drawn

options.text: The sites change because each ligand breaks the protein apart slightly.
options.misconception: reads a conformational change as damage

questions.explanation: The widening of successive sites shows that earlier ligand binding primes the remaining sites, so occupancy rises faster than it would with independent sites. That is cooperative behaviour in a multimeric protein.
questions.hint: Track what changes about the site after each ligand.
